newsitem.title: MALTA: Malta votes for Labour and against European Union.
newsitem.headline: Malta votes for Labour and against European Union.

text.p: In a remarkable upset election victory for the Labour Party sealed on Monday, the people of Malta rejected membership of the European Union and the Mediterranean island's VAT taxation system.

Labour leader Alfred Sant, 48, claimed victory on Sunday as votes were counted in a general election focused on his party's pledge to scrap the highly unpopular Value Added Tax and end Malta's bid to join Europe.
Former Nationalist Party prime minister Edward Fenech Adami accepted defeat.
"Dr Fenech Adami informed the president of Malta that he accepted victory of the Labour Party early on Monday morning," a party spokesman told Reuters.
Official results from the poll which drew a record 97 percent of the near 275,000 electorate were being given to President Ugo Mifsud Bonnici later in the day.
Blasts from fireworks reverberated through the ancient streets of the capital Valletta as drivers of cars decked with red Labour flags celebrated into the morning.
Under Sant's leadership, Malta can be expected to forge closer ties with North Africa, including Libya with whom it traditionally has close relations.

"We want a special relationship with Europe but I argue that you start with your neighbours," he said, adding that he wanted friendly relations with Libya but would adhere to U.N. sanctions imposed on Tripoli over the Lockerbie aircraft bombing.
Except for VAT and pulling out of NATO's Partnership for Peace Programme, Sant was not expected to roll back on many of the changes introduced under Fenech Adami's preparations for EU membership.

"In the longer term, Labour has commitments with Europe and there will be a need for many discussions between Malta and the EU to have the close relationship Sant talks about," said one foreign political analyst, who asked not to be named.
"They (Labour) are also committed to have Malta as a financial centre and will want to maintain the confidence of the financial community," he added.

The Times newspaper termed the result, in which Labour overturned a record Nationalist majority of 13,000 votes and three-seat majority in the 65-member parliament, "the biggest upset for a quarter of a century".
Sant, who transformed his party's image from a violence-prone centre of radicalism to appeal to middle-ground voters, promised a government "for all the people".

Fenech Adami had pledged to pursue his 1990 application to join the EU, which he had forecast could be completed by mid-1998. In calling elections eight months early, he gambled on his management of the economy which had seen growth around six percent a year and unemployment cut.
On the Partnership for Peace, which Malta joined last year, Sant told Reuters earlier that his party opposed a return to a fortress island.

He was unhappy about the increased visits by Western naval vessels to Malta -- awarded the British George Cross in 1942 for bravery withstanding Italian and German wartime attacks. He said pulling out of the Partnership "will be my first priority".
It would be followed by legislation to abolish VAT and replace it with customs tariffs, undercutting a basis of EU membership and signalling Malta's withdrawal of its bid.

Discontent with VAT, with a standard rate of 15 percent, has been widespread, both for its impact on inflation, running officially at around four percent, and for perceived meddling by officialdom in traditionally secretive family businesses.
Sant says he wants Malta to have a "positive neutrality" and only a "special relationship" and free trade agreement with Europe, instead of EU membership.
